scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance traces its lineage to the ancient period of the Ramayana.
It is historically regarded as the dance of the Vanara (monkey) army, created to celebrate the victory of Rama over Ravana.
It has been preserved in the region of Puducherry (formerly Pondicherry) as a traditional folk form.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Garadi is a ceremonial dance performed to celebrate divine victory.
Its primary occasion is the car festival of Lord Vishnu, where it serves as a ritual offering and public celebration.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by intricate movements that focus on the legs to activate the iron rings.
It is a high-endurance form, with performances lasting between five and eight hours per night.
Dancers must manage the weight of twenty iron rings while maintaining rhythmic synchronization.
Watch for Anjali striking.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary sound of the dance is produced by the 'anjali' (iron rings) worn by the dancers.
Ten rings are worn on each leg.
Listen for the Anjali (iron rings), Drums.
The sound is dominated by the rhythmic, metallic jingling and clanging of twenty iron rings striking together with every step, layered over a foundation of traditional drumming.
